common_name: Blue Globe Globe Thistle (Classic Blue-Grey Echinops)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or set out transplants in spring, in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Globe is a deep-rooted taprooted selection that resents disturbance once established, so choose its permanent spot carefully.

directions: Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Globe is the most widely grown Echinops bannaticus selection, producing the classic perfectly round, steel-blue-grey flower spheres on stiff, branching stems above spiny, deeply cut leaves that are dark green above and downy white beneath. Cutting spent stems back after the first flush often coaxes a second, lighter bloom in early fall. Bumblebees and other long-tongued pollinators visit the globe-shaped flower heads heavily through summer, and the dried heads are long-lasting in arrangements. Once established in lean, well-drained soil the deep taproot makes the plant extremely drought-tolerant but very difficult to divide or move.

common_name: Platinum Blue Globe Thistle (Silvery Compact Echinops)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or set out transplants in spring, in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; Platinum Blue stays a tidy, clump-forming size and rarely needs staking despite its silvery, branched flowering stems.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Platinum Blue is a compact globe thistle selection with striking silvery-green, finely cut foliage that sets off bright, metallic-blue spherical flower heads carried on tall, silvery, branched stems in late summer. The frosted foliage color makes this selection read as noticeably brighter and cooler than green-leaved Echinops ritro cultivars, and it pairs especially well with other silver-leaved and blue-flowered border plants. Bees work the spherical flower heads steadily through the peak of summer, and the whole plant is exceptionally drought-tolerant once its deep taproot is established. Avoid rich, moist soils, which cause lax, floppy growth in this naturally lean-soil species.

common_name: Jade Frost Sea Holly (Variegated Cream-Margined Eryngium)

planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring into dry, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Jade Frost is a patented variegated sport that must be propagated vegetatively, since seedlings will not come true to its cream-edged foliage.

directions: Plant in dry, sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun; Jade Frost stands apart from other sea hollies for its foliage as much as its flowers — the blue-green basal leaves carry bold, creamy-white margins that emerge flushed pink in cool spring and autumn weather before settling to cream. In summer, wiry violet-blue stems rise above the rosette carrying small, egg-shaped, silvery-blue flower heads typical of the species. The variegated foliage provides season-long interest even between bloom flushes, making it a useful accent among green-leaved perennials and ornamental grasses. Like other sea hollies it develops a long taproot and is extremely drought-tolerant once established, but performs poorly in heavy, wet, or rich soil.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall without stratification, or set out started plants in spring, into lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Blaukappe (German for 'blue cap') is an older, reliable seed strain valued for its consistently deep blue color.

directions: Grow in lean, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Blaukappe is a long-cultivated German selection of flat sea holly prized for its saturated, deep steel-blue flower heads and bracts, produced on sturdy branching stems from midsummer into early fall. It is one of the most heavily visited Eryngium selections by bees of all kinds, and the extended bloom period keeps pollinators returning for weeks at a stretch. Like the species, Blaukappe develops a deep taproot and dislikes being moved once settled, so site it where it can remain undisturbed. Cut stems for fresh or dried arrangements just as the color peaks, since the metallic-blue bracts hold their color for months after drying.

common_name: Blue Hobbit Sea Holly (Dwarf Steely-Blue Eryngium)

planting.note: Set out started plants or direct sow in spring into sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun; Blue Hobbit is a genuine dwarf strain and needs a sunny, lean site to keep its compact mounded habit and best blue color.

directions: Plant in free-draining, lean, sandy soil in full sun; Blue Hobbit is a true genetic dwarf sea holly, forming a compact rosette of toothed leaves topped by a profusion of small, spiny, purplish-blue flower heads on silvery-blue stems that rarely exceed a foot in height even at peak bloom. The sunnier the site, the more intense the blue coloring becomes, making it ideal for the front of a gravel garden, rock garden, or container where taller sea hollies would overwhelm the space. It tolerates coastal exposure and clay soil better than many Eryngium selections, provided drainage is adequate. Bees, butterflies, and other pollinators visit the flower heads steadily through summer, and the spent heads can be left standing for winter texture.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Bleeding Hearts flowers most intensely and holds its sturdy, black-tinged stems best with a full day of direct sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil of average fertility in full sun; Bleeding Hearts is a striking departure from typical false sunflower, carrying deep purple-black stems and bronze-tinged foliage that set off flowers with no yellow in them at all — buds open an intense scarlet-red-orange and gradually mature to a warmer golden-orange, so a single plant in full bloom shows several flower colors simultaneously. Flowering runs from midsummer until hard frost, making it one of the longest-blooming heliopsis selections available. The sturdy, dark stems resist flopping even under a heavy bloom load, reducing the need for staking. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor, and deadhead through the season to keep new buds coming.

common_name: Prairie Sunset False Sunflower (Maroon-Eyed Gold Heliopsis)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Prairie Sunset tolerates both dry and consistently moist soils better than many heliopsis selections.

directions: Grow in well-drained soil of average fertility in full sun to light shade; Prairie Sunset is a Neil Diboll introduction selected for its deep purple stems and purple-veined foliage, which contrast strongly with masses of golden-yellow daisy flowers marked by a distinctive dark red-maroon ring at the base of the petals surrounding the central disc. Vigorous, quick-forming clumps stay upright without staking and bloom from midsummer well into fall, drawing butterflies and other pollinators steadily throughout the season. It is more tolerant of both dry spells and periods of wet soil than many heliopsis selections, making it a reliable choice for rain gardens as well as average borders. The gold-and-maroon flowers are long-lasting as cut flowers.

common_name: Jim Crockett Boltonia (Compact Violet-Rayed False Aster)

planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring after the danger of hard frost, in full sun with reliably moist soil; Jim Crockett stays compact and self-supporting so it rarely needs the staking taller boltonias require.

directions: Plant in moist to average, fertile soil in full sun; Jim Crockett is a compact selection of native false aster, introduced from a University of Massachusetts breeding program and named for the original host of public television's The Victory Garden. It stays under two feet tall, far shorter than the species' five to six feet, while still smothering itself in one-and-a-half-inch, violet-rayed, yellow-centered daisy flowers from August into September. Its dark green, free-branching foliage shows good resistance to the powdery mildew that can disfigure taller boltonia selections late in the season. The compact habit makes it useful toward the middle of a moist, sunny border where a full-sized boltonia would overwhelm neighboring perennials, and its late bloom is valuable to migrating monarchs and other pollinators.

common_name: Nally's Lime Dot Boltonia (Chartreuse Button-Flowered False Aster)

planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring in full sun with reliably moist soil; cut stems back by about a third in early summer to keep this tall selection from flopping under its late-season bloom load.

directions: Plant in moist to average, fertile soil in full sun; Nally's Lime Dot is an unusual selection of native false aster named for horticulturist John Nally of Wave Hill garden, grown not for showy petals but for its distinctive flowers — the ray florets are absent or greatly reduced, so the plant produces masses of small, button-like, chartreuse-green flower heads that float above blue-green foliage on tall stems from September into October. The lime-green color and unusual petal-less form make it a favorite of flower arrangers and a striking contrast plant among more conventionally showy late-season perennials. At four to six feet, stems can lean or flop under the weight of bloom in rich soil, so cutting the clump back by about a third in early summer produces a shorter, sturdier, more floriferous plant. It shares the species' tolerance for consistently moist soil and is valuable to late-season pollinators.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
